141|## CORSMiddleware
142|
143|Adds appropriate [CORS headers](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS) to outgoing responses in order to allow cross-origin requests from browsers.
144|
145|The default parameters used by the CORSMiddleware implementation are restrictive by default,
146|so you'll need to explicitly enable particular origins, methods, or headers, in order
147|for browsers to be permitted to use them in a Cross-Domain context.
148|
149|```python
150|from starlette.applications import Starlette
151|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
152|from starlette.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
153|
154|routes = ...
155|
156|middleware = [
157|    Middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=['*'])
158|]
159|
160|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
161|```
162|
163|The following arguments are supported:
164|
165|* `allow_origins` - A list of origins that should be permitted to make cross-origin requests. eg. `['https://example.org', 'https://www.example.org']`. You can use `['*']` to allow any origin.
166|* `allow_origin_regex` - A regex string to match against origins that should be permitted to make cross-origin requests. eg. `'https://[a-zA-Z0-9-]+\.example\.org'`. Avoid using `.*` or `.+` as they match URL special characters (`/`, `@`, `#`, `?`) and may result in overly permissive origin matching. Use specific character classes like `[a-zA-Z0-9-]+` instead.
167|* `allow_methods` - A list of HTTP methods that should be allowed for cross-origin requests. Defaults to `['GET']`. You can use `['*']` to allow all standard methods.
168|* `allow_headers` - A list of HTTP request headers that should be supported for cross-origin requests. Defaults to `[]`. You can use `['*']` to allow all headers. The `Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Content-Language` and `Content-Type` headers are always allowed for CORS requests.
169|* `allow_credentials` - Indicate that cookies should be supported for cross-origin requests. Defaults to `False`. Also, `allow_origins`, `allow_methods` and `allow_headers` cannot be set to `['*']` for credentials to be allowed, all of them must be explicitly specified.
170|* `allow_private_network` - Indicates whether to accept cross-origin requests over a private network. Defaults to `False`.
171|* `expose_headers` - Indicate any response headers that should be made accessible to the browser. Defaults to `[]`.
172|* `max_age` - Sets a maximum time in seconds for browsers to cache CORS responses. Defaults to `600`.
173|
174|The middleware responds to two particular types of HTTP request...
175|
176|#### CORS preflight requests
177|
178|These are any `OPTIONS` request with `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method` headers.
179|In this case the middleware will intercept the incoming request and respond with
180|appropriate CORS headers, and either a 200 or 400 response for informational purposes.
181|
182|#### Simple requests
183|
184|Any request with an `Origin` header. In this case the middleware will pass the
185|request through as normal, but will include appropriate CORS headers on the response.
186|
187|#### Private Network Access (PNA)
188|
189|Private Network Access is a browser security feature that restricts websites from public networks from accessing servers on private networks.
190|
191|When a website attempts to make such a cross-network request, the browser will send a `Access-Control-Request-Private-Network: true` header in the
192|pre-flight request. If the `allow_private_network` flag is set to `True`, the middleware will include the `Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network: true`
193|header in the response, allowing the request. If set to `False`, the middleware will return a 400 response, blocking the request.
194|
195|### CORSMiddleware Global Enforcement
196|
197|When using CORSMiddleware with your Starlette application, it's important to ensure that CORS headers are applied even to error responses generated by unhandled exceptions. The recommended solution is to wrap the entire Starlette application with CORSMiddleware. This approach guarantees that even if an exception is caught by ServerErrorMiddleware (or other outer error-handling middleware), the response will still include the proper `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header.
198|
199|For example, instead of adding CORSMiddleware as an inner `middleware` via the Starlette middleware parameter, you can wrap your application as follows:
200|
201|```python
202|from starlette.applications import Starlette
203|from starlette.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
204|
205|import uvicorn
206|
207|app = Starlette()
208|app = CORSMiddleware(app=app, allow_origins=["*"])
209|
210|# ... your routes and middleware configuration ...
211|
212|if __name__ == '__main__':
213|    uvicorn.run(
214|        app,
215|        host='0.0.0.0',
216|        port=8000
217|    )
218|```
219|
220|## SessionMiddleware
221|
222|Adds signed cookie-based HTTP sessions. Session information is readable but not modifiable.
223|
224|The session cookie is always set with the `"HttpOnly"` flag, preventing client-side JavaScript from accessing it.
225|
226|Access or modify the session data using the `request.session` dictionary interface.
227|
228|Changes to nested values are not tracked automatically. For example, `request.session["cart"].append(item)` does not mark the session as modified. Assign the updated value back to the session, such as `request.session["cart"] = cart`, to ensure the changes are saved.
229|
230|The following arguments are supported:
231|
232|* `secret_key` - Should be a random string.
233|* `session_cookie` - Defaults to "session".
234|* `max_age` - Session expiry time in seconds. Defaults to 2 weeks. If set to `None` then the cookie will last as long as the browser session.
235|* `same_site` - SameSite flag prevents the browser from sending session cookie along with cross-site requests. Defaults to `'lax'`.
236|* `path` - The path set for the session cookie. Defaults to `'/'`.
237|* `https_only` - Indicate that the `"Secure"` flag should be set (can be used with HTTPS only). Defaults to `False`. Set this to `True` in production to ensure the session cookie is only sent over HTTPS.
238|* `domain` - Domain of the cookie used to share cookie between subdomains or cross-domains. The browser defaults the domain to the same host that set the cookie, excluding subdomains ([reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Cookies#domain_attribute)).
239|* `partitioned` - Set the `Partitioned` flag when you write or clear the session cookie. Defaults to `False`. Set `https_only=True` when you enable it. For cross-site embeds, also set `same_site="none"`. This gives your embedded app a separate session for each top-level site ([reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Privacy/Guides/Third-party_cookies/Partitioned_cookies)).
240|
241|
242|```python
243|from starlette.applications import Starlette
244|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
245|from starlette.middleware.sessions import SessionMiddleware
246|
247|routes = ...
248|
249|middleware = [
250|    Middleware(SessionMiddleware, secret_key=..., https_only=True)
251|]
252|
253|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
254|```
255|
256|## HTTPSRedirectMiddleware
257|
258|Enforces that all incoming requests must either be `https` or `wss`. Any incoming
259|requests to `http` or `ws` will be redirected to the secure scheme instead.
260|
261|```python
262|from starlette.applications import Starlette
263|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
264|from starlette.middleware.httpsredirect import HTTPSRedirectMiddleware
265|
266|routes = ...
267|
268|middleware = [
269|    Middleware(HTTPSRedirectMiddleware)
270|]
271|
272|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
273|```
274|
275|There are no configuration options for this middleware class.
276|
277|## TrustedHostMiddleware
278|
279|Enforces that all incoming requests have a correctly set `Host` header, in order
280|to guard against HTTP Host Header attacks.
281|
282|```python
283|from starlette.applications import Starlette
284|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
285|from starlette.middleware.trustedhost import TrustedHostMiddleware
286|
287|routes = ...
288|
289|middleware = [
290|    Middleware(TrustedHostMiddleware, allowed_hosts=['example.com', '*.example.com'])
291|]
292|
293|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
294|```
295|
296|The following arguments are supported:
297|
298|* `allowed_hosts` - A list of domain names that should be allowed as hostnames. Wildcard
299|domains such as `*.example.com` are supported for matching subdomains. Use bracketed
300|notation for IPv6 addresses, such as `allowed_hosts=["[::1]"]`. To allow any hostname,
301|use `allowed_hosts=["*"]` or omit the middleware.
302|* `www_redirect` - If set to True, requests to non-www versions of the allowed hosts will be redirected to their www counterparts. Defaults to `True`.
303|
304|If an incoming request does not validate correctly then a 400 response will be sent.
305|
306|## RequestBodyLimitMiddleware
307|
308|Limits the total size of incoming HTTP request bodies. The limit applies to the
309|raw body bytes, including multipart file data and multipart encoding overhead.
310|Requests that exceed the limit receive a `413 Content Too Large` response.
311|
312|```python
313|from starlette.applications import Starlette
314|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
315|from starlette.middleware.body_limit import RequestBodyLimitMiddleware
316|
317|
318|routes = ...
319|
320|middleware = [
321|    Middleware(RequestBodyLimitMiddleware, max_body_size=10 * 1024 * 1024)
322|]
323|
324|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
325|```
326|
327|The following argument is supported:
328|
329|* `max_body_size` - The non-negative maximum request body size in bytes.
330|
331|The middleware uses `Content-Length` to reject an oversized body before reading
332|it when possible, and always counts the body bytes received from the ASGI server.
333|This also supports requests without `Content-Length` and prevents an understated
334|header from bypassing the limit.
335|
336|## GZipMiddleware
337|
338|Handles GZip responses for any request that includes `"gzip"` in the `Accept-Encoding` header.
339|
340|The middleware will handle both standard and streaming responses.
341|
342|??? info "Compression of streaming responses"
343|    On streaming responses, the middleware compresses and emits output for every chunk the application sends,
344|    so chunks reach the client as they are produced instead of waiting for the compressor's buffer to fill.
345|
346|    This favors timely delivery over compression ratio: many small chunks compress less effectively than a few
347|    large ones. Batch the chunks you yield if you want to maximize compression.
348|
349|```python
350|from starlette.applications import Starlette
351|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
352|from starlette.middleware.gzip import GZipMiddleware
353|
354|
355|routes = ...
356|
357|middleware = [
358|    Middleware(GZipMiddleware, minimum_size=1000, compresslevel=9)
359|]
360|
361|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
362|```
363|
364|The following arguments are supported:
365|
366|* `minimum_size` - Do not GZip responses that are smaller than this minimum size in bytes. Defaults to `500`.
367|* `compresslevel` - Used during GZip compression. It is an integer ranging from 1 to 9. Defaults to `9`. Lower value results in faster compression but larger file sizes, while higher value results in slower compression but smaller file sizes.
368|* `thread_minimum_size` - Compress body chunks at least this large in a worker thread, keeping the event loop responsive. Defaults to `131072` (128 KiB). Chunks below this size compress inline in at most a couple of milliseconds, while the fixed cost of dispatching to a worker thread would dominate.
369|* `exclude_content_types` - Content types that are never compressed. A response is excluded when its `Content-Type` media type equals one of these values, or matches a `type/*` entry like `"image/*"` - matching is case-insensitive and ignores parameters like `charset`. Defaults to `DEFAULT_EXCLUDED_CONTENT_TYPES` (importable, to extend rather than replace): `text/event-stream`, native gRPC (`application/grpc`, which also covers `application/grpc+proto` and other `application/grpc+...` subtypes), plus already-compressed formats - zip and gzip archives, common raster image types, `video/*`, `audio/*`, and WOFF fonts. `image/svg+xml` is deliberately not excluded, since SVG is text and compresses well.
370|
371|The middleware won't GZip responses that already have a `Content-Encoding` set, to prevent them from being
372|encoded twice, partial content responses (status `206`), to keep range semantics
373|intact, or responses with a `Content-Type` in `exclude_content_types` - by default `text/event-stream`, to
374|avoid compressing server-sent events, and already-compressed formats, where compression wastes CPU for no
375|gain.
376|
377|## BaseHTTPMiddleware
378|
379|An abstract class that allows you to write ASGI middleware against a request/response
380|interface.
381|
382|### Usage
383|
384|To implement a middleware class using `BaseHTTPMiddleware`, you must override the
385|`async def dispatch(request, call_next)` method.
386|
387|```python
388|from starlette.applications import Starlette
389|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
390|from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
391|
392|
393|class CustomHeaderMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
394|    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
395|        response = await call_next(request)
396|        response.headers['Custom'] = 'Example'
397|        return response
398|
399|routes = ...
400|
401|middleware = [
402|    Middleware(CustomHeaderMiddleware)
403|]
404|
405|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
406|```
407|
408|If you want to provide configuration options to the middleware class you should
409|override the `__init__` method, ensuring that the first argument is `app`, and
410|any remaining arguments are optional keyword arguments. Make sure to set the `app`
411|attribute on the instance if you do this.
412|
413|```python
414|class CustomHeaderMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
415|    def __init__(self, app, header_value='Example'):
416|        super().__init__(app)
417|        self.header_value = header_value
418|
419|    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
420|        response = await call_next(request)
421|        response.headers['Custom'] = self.header_value
422|        return response
423|
424|
425|middleware = [
426|    Middleware(CustomHeaderMiddleware, header_value='Customized')
427|]
428|
429|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
430|```
431|
432|Middleware classes should not modify their state outside of the `__init__` method.
433|Instead you should keep any state local to the `dispatch` method, or pass it
434|around explicitly, rather than mutating the middleware instance.
435|
436|### Limitations
437|
438|Currently, the `BaseHTTPMiddleware` has some known limitations:
439|
440|- Using `BaseHTTPMiddleware` will prevent changes to [`contextvars.ContextVar`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextvars.html#contextvars.ContextVar)s from propagating upwards. That is, if you set a value for a `ContextVar` in your endpoint and try to read it from a middleware you will find that the value is not the same value you set in your endpoint (see [this test](https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/blob/621abc747a6604825190b93467918a0ec6456a24/tests/middleware/test_base.py#L192-L223) for an example of this behavior). Importantly, this also means that if a `BaseHTTPMiddleware` is positioned earlier in the middleware stack, it will disrupt `contextvars` propagation for any subsequent Pure ASGI Middleware that relies on them.
441|
442|To overcome these limitations, use [pure ASGI middleware](#pure-asgi-middleware), as shown below.
443|
444|## Pure ASGI Middleware
445|
446|The [ASGI spec](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) makes it possible to implement ASGI middleware using the ASGI interface directly, as a chain of ASGI applications that call into the next one. In fact, this is how middleware classes shipped with Starlette are implemented.
447|
448|This lower-level approach provides greater control over behavior and enhanced interoperability across frameworks and servers. It also overcomes the [limitations of `BaseHTTPMiddleware`](#limitations).
449|
450|### Writing pure ASGI middleware
451|
452|The most common way to create an ASGI middleware is with a class.
453|
454|```python
455|class ASGIMiddleware:
456|    def __init__(self, app):
457|        self.app = app
458|
459|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
460|        await self.app(scope, receive, send)
461|```
462|
463|The middleware above is the most basic ASGI middleware. It receives a parent ASGI application as an argument for its constructor, and implements an `async __call__` method which calls into that parent application.
464|
465|Some implementations such as [`asgi-cors`](https://github.com/simonw/asgi-cors/blob/10ef64bfcc6cd8d16f3014077f20a0fb8544ec39/asgi_cors.py) use an alternative style, using functions:
466|
467|```python
468|import functools
469|
470|def asgi_middleware():
471|    def asgi_decorator(app):
472|
473|        @functools.wraps(app)
474|        async def wrapped_app(scope, receive, send):
475|            await app(scope, receive, send)
476|
477|        return wrapped_app
478|
479|    return asgi_decorator
480|```
481|
482|In any case, ASGI middleware must be callables that accept three arguments: `scope`, `receive`, and `send`.
483|
484|* `scope` is a dict holding information about the connection, where `scope["type"]` may be:
485|    * [`"http"`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#http-connection-scope): for HTTP requests.
486|    * [`"websocket"`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#websocket-connection-scope): for WebSocket connections.
487|    * [`"lifespan"`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/lifespan.html#scope): for ASGI lifespan messages.
488|* `receive` and `send` can be used to exchange ASGI event messages with the ASGI server — more on this below. The type and contents of these messages depend on the scope type. Learn more in the [ASGI specification](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/index.html).
489|
490|### Using pure ASGI middleware
491|
492|Pure ASGI middleware can be used like any other middleware:
493|
494|```python
495|from starlette.applications import Starlette
496|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
497|
498|from .middleware import ASGIMiddleware
499|
500|routes = ...
501|
502|middleware = [
503|    Middleware(ASGIMiddleware),
504|]
505|
506|app = Starlette(..., middleware=middleware)
507|```
508|
509|See also [Using middleware](#using-middleware).
510|
511|### Type annotations
512|
513|There are two ways of annotating a middleware: using Starlette itself or [`asgiref`](https://github.com/django/asgiref).
514|
515|* Using Starlette: for most common use cases.
516|
517|```python
518|from starlette.types import ASGIApp, Message, Scope, Receive, Send
519|
520|
521|class ASGIMiddleware:
522|    def __init__(self, app: ASGIApp) -> None:
523|        self.app = app
524|
525|    async def __call__(self, scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send) -> None:
526|        if scope["type"] != "http":
527|            return await self.app(scope, receive, send)
528|
529|        async def send_wrapper(message: Message) -> None:
530|            # ... Do something
531|            await send(message)
532|
533|        await self.app(scope, receive, send_wrapper)
534|```
535|
536|* Using [`asgiref`](https://github.com/django/asgiref): for more rigorous type hinting.
537|
538|```python
539|from asgiref.typing import ASGI3Application, ASGIReceiveCallable, ASGISendCallable, Scope
540|from asgiref.typing import ASGIReceiveEvent, ASGISendEvent
541|
542|
543|class ASGIMiddleware:
544|    def __init__(self, app: ASGI3Application) -> None:
545|        self.app = app
546|
547|    async def __call__(self, scope: Scope, receive: ASGIReceiveCallable, send: ASGISendCallable) -> None:
548|        if scope["type"] != "http":
549|            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
550|            return
551|
552|        async def send_wrapper(message: ASGISendEvent) -> None:
553|            # ... Do something
554|            await send(message)
555|
556|        return await self.app(scope, receive, send_wrapper)
557|```
558|
559|### Common patterns
560|
561|#### Processing certain requests only
562|
563|ASGI middleware can apply specific behavior according to the contents of `scope`.
564|
565|For example, to only process HTTP requests, write this...
566|
567|```python
568|class ASGIMiddleware:
569|    def __init__(self, app):
570|        self.app = app
571|
572|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
573|        if scope["type"] != "http":
574|            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
575|            return
576|
577|        ...  # Do something here!
578|
579|        await self.app(scope, receive, send)
580|```
581|
582|Likewise, WebSocket-only middleware would guard on `scope["type"] != "websocket"`.
583|
584|The middleware may also act differently based on the request method, URL, headers, etc.
585|
586|#### Reusing Starlette components
587|
588|Starlette provides several data structures that accept the ASGI `scope`, `receive` and/or `send` arguments, allowing you to work at a higher level of abstraction. Such data structures include [`Request`](requests.md#request), [`Headers`](requests.md#headers), [`QueryParams`](requests.md#query-parameters), [`URL`](requests.md#url), etc.
589|
590|For example, you can instantiate a `Request` to more easily inspect an HTTP request:
591|
592|```python
593|from starlette.requests import Request
594|
595|class ASGIMiddleware:
596|    def __init__(self, app):
597|        self.app = app
598|
599|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
600|        if scope["type"] == "http":
601|            request = Request(scope)
602|            ... # Use `request.method`, `request.url`, `request.headers`, etc.
603|
604|        await self.app(scope, receive, send)
605|```
606|
607|You can also reuse [responses](responses.md), which are ASGI applications as well.
608|
609|#### Sending eager responses
610|
611|Inspecting the connection `scope` allows you to conditionally call into a different ASGI app. One use case might be sending a response without calling into the app.
612|
613|As an example, this middleware uses a dictionary to perform permanent redirects based on the requested path. This could be used to implement ongoing support of legacy URLs in case you need to refactor route URL patterns.
614|
615|```python
616|from starlette.datastructures import URL
617|from starlette.responses import RedirectResponse
618|
619|class RedirectsMiddleware:
620|    def __init__(self, app, path_mapping: dict):
621|        self.app = app
622|        self.path_mapping = path_mapping
623|
624|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
625|        if scope["type"] != "http":
626|            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
627|            return
628|
629|        url = URL(scope=scope)
630|
631|        if url.path in self.path_mapping:
632|            url = url.replace(path=self.path_mapping[url.path])
633|            response = RedirectResponse(url, status_code=301)
634|            await response(scope, receive, send)
635|            return
636|
637|        await self.app(scope, receive, send)
638|```
639|
640|Example usage would look like this:
641|
642|```python
643|from starlette.applications import Starlette
644|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
645|
646|routes = ...
647|
648|redirections = {
649|    "/v1/resource/": "/v2/resource/",
650|    # ...
651|}
652|
653|middleware = [
654|    Middleware(RedirectsMiddleware, path_mapping=redirections),
655|]
656|
657|app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
658|```
659|
660|
661|#### Inspecting or modifying the request
662|
663|Request information can be accessed or changed by manipulating the `scope`. For a full example of this pattern, see Uvicorn's [`ProxyHeadersMiddleware`](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/fd4386fefb8fe8a4568831a7d8b2930d5fb61455/uvicorn/middleware/proxy_headers.py) which inspects and tweaks the `scope` when serving behind a frontend proxy.
664|
665|Besides, wrapping the `receive` ASGI callable allows you to access or modify the HTTP request body by manipulating [`http.request`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#request-receive-event) ASGI event messages.
666|
667|As an example, this middleware computes and logs the size of the incoming request body...
668|
669|```python
670|class LoggedRequestBodySizeMiddleware:
671|    def __init__(self, app):
672|        self.app = app
673|
674|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
675|        if scope["type"] != "http":
676|            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
677|            return
678|
679|        body_size = 0
680|
681|        async def receive_logging_request_body_size():
682|            nonlocal body_size
683|
684|            message = await receive()
685|            assert message["type"] == "http.request"
686|
687|            body_size += len(message.get("body", b""))
688|
689|            if not message.get("more_body", False):
690|                print(f"Size of request body was: {body_size} bytes")
691|
692|            return message
693|
694|        await self.app(scope, receive_logging_request_body_size, send)
695|```
696|
697|Likewise, WebSocket middleware may manipulate [`websocket.receive`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#receive-receive-event) ASGI event messages to inspect or alter incoming WebSocket data.
698|
699|For an example that changes the HTTP request body, see [`msgpack-asgi`](https://github.com/florimondmanca/msgpack-asgi).
700|
701|#### Inspecting or modifying the response
702|
703|Wrapping the `send` ASGI callable allows you to inspect or modify the HTTP response sent by the underlying application. To do so, react to [`http.response.start`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#response-start-send-event) or [`http.response.body`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#response-body-send-event) ASGI event messages.
704|
705|As an example, this middleware adds some fixed extra response headers:
706|
707|```python
708|from starlette.datastructures import MutableHeaders
709|
710|class ExtraResponseHeadersMiddleware:
711|    def __init__(self, app, headers):
712|        self.app = app
713|        self.headers = headers
714|
715|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
716|        if scope["type"] != "http":
717|            return await self.app(scope, receive, send)
718|
719|        async def send_with_extra_headers(message):
720|            if message["type"] == "http.response.start":
721|                headers = MutableHeaders(scope=message)
722|                for key, value in self.headers:
723|                    headers.append(key, value)
724|
725|            await send(message)
726|
727|        await self.app(scope, receive, send_with_extra_headers)
728|```
729|
730|See also [`asgi-logger`](https://github.com/Kludex/asgi-logger/blob/main/asgi_logger/middleware.py) for an example that inspects the HTTP response and logs a configurable HTTP access log line.
731|
732|Likewise, WebSocket middleware may manipulate [`websocket.send`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#send-send-event) ASGI event messages to inspect or alter outgoing WebSocket data.
733|
734|Note that if you change the response body, you will need to update the response `Content-Length` header to match the new response body length. See [`brotli-asgi`](https://github.com/fullonic/brotli-asgi) for a complete example.
735|
736|#### Passing information to endpoints
737|
738|If you need to share information with the underlying app or endpoints, you may store it into the `scope` dictionary. Note that this is a convention -- for example, Starlette uses this to share routing information with endpoints -- but it is not part of the ASGI specification. If you do so, be sure to avoid conflicts by using keys that have low chances of being used by other middleware or applications.
739|
740|For example, when including the middleware below, endpoints would be able to access `request.scope["asgi_transaction_id"]`.
741|
742|```python
743|import uuid
744|
745|class TransactionIDMiddleware:
746|    def __init__(self, app):
747|        self.app = app
748|
749|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
750|        scope["asgi_transaction_id"] = uuid.uuid4()
751|        await self.app(scope, receive, send)
752|```
753|
754|#### Cleanup and error handling
755|
756|You can wrap the application in a `try/except/finally` block or a context manager to perform cleanup operations or do error handling.
757|
758|For example, the following middleware might collect metrics and process application exceptions...
759|
760|```python
761|import time
762|
763|class MonitoringMiddleware:
764|    def __init__(self, app):
765|        self.app = app
766|
767|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
768|        start = time.time()
769|        try:
770|            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
771|        except Exception as exc:
772|            ...  # Process the exception
773|            raise
774|        finally:
775|            end = time.time()
776|            elapsed = end - start
777|            ...  # Submit `elapsed` as a metric to a monitoring backend
778|```
779|
780|See also [`timing-asgi`](https://github.com/steinnes/timing-asgi) for a full example of this pattern.
781|
782|### Gotchas
783|
784|#### ASGI middleware should be stateless
785|
786|Because ASGI is designed to handle concurrent requests, any connection-specific state should be scoped to the `__call__` implementation. Not doing so would typically lead to conflicting variable reads/writes across requests, and most likely bugs.
787|
788|As an example, this would conditionally replace the response body, if an `X-Mock` header is present in the response...
789|
790|=== "✅ Do"
791|
792|    ```python
793|    from starlette.datastructures import Headers
794|
795|    class MockResponseBodyMiddleware:
796|        def __init__(self, app, content):
797|            self.app = app
798|            self.content = content
799|
800|        async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
801|            if scope["type"] != "http":
802|                await self.app(scope, receive, send)
803|                return
804|
805|            # A flag that we will turn `True` if the HTTP response
806|            # has the 'X-Mock' header.
807|            # ✅: Scoped to this function.
808|            should_mock = False
809|
810|            async def maybe_send_with_mock_content(message):
811|                nonlocal should_mock
812|
813|                if message["type"] == "http.response.start":
814|                    headers = Headers(raw=message["headers"])
815|                    should_mock = headers.get("X-Mock") == "1"
816|                    await send(message)
817|
818|                elif message["type"] == "http.response.body":
819|                    if should_mock:
820|                        message = {"type": "http.response.body", "body": self.content}
821|                    await send(message)
822|
823|            await self.app(scope, receive, maybe_send_with_mock_content)
824|    ```
825|
826|=== "❌ Don't"
827|
828|    ```python hl_lines="7-8"
829|    from starlette.datastructures import Headers
830|
831|    class MockResponseBodyMiddleware:
832|        def __init__(self, app, content):
833|            self.app = app
834|            self.content = content
835|            # ❌: This variable would be read and written across requests!
836|            self.should_mock = False
837|
838|        async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
839|            if scope["type"] != "http":
840|                await self.app(scope, receive, send)
841|                return
842|
843|            async def maybe_send_with_mock_content(message):
844|                if message["type"] == "http.response.start":
845|                    headers = Headers(raw=message["headers"])
846|                    self.should_mock = headers.get("X-Mock") == "1"
847|                    await send(message)
848|
849|                elif message["type"] == "http.response.body":
850|                    if self.should_mock:
851|                        message = {"type": "http.response.body", "body": self.content}
852|                    await send(message)
853|
854|            await self.app(scope, receive, maybe_send_with_mock_content)
855|    ```
856|
857|See also [`GZipMiddleware`](https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/blob/9ef1b91c9c043197da6c3f38aa153fd874b95527/starlette/middleware/gzip.py) for a full example implementation that navigates this potential gotcha.
858|
859|### Further reading
860|
861|This documentation should be enough to have a good basis on how to create an ASGI middleware.
862|
863|Nonetheless, there are great articles about the subject:
864|
865|- [Introduction to ASGI: Emergence of an Async Python Web Ecosystem](https://florimond.dev/en/posts/2019/08/introduction-to-asgi-async-python-web/)
866|- [How to write ASGI middleware](https://pgjones.dev/blog/how-to-write-asgi-middleware-2021/)
867|
868|## Using middleware in other frameworks
869|
870|To wrap ASGI middleware around other ASGI applications, you should use the
871|more general pattern of wrapping the application instance:
872|
873|```python
874|app = TrustedHostMiddleware(app, allowed_hosts=['example.com'])
875|```
876|
877|You can do this with a Starlette application instance too, but it is preferable
878|to use the `middleware=<List of Middleware instances>` style, as it will:
879|
880|* Ensure that everything remains wrapped in a single outermost `ServerErrorMiddleware`.
881|* Preserves the top-level `app` instance.
882|
883|## Applying middleware to groups of routes
884|
885|Middleware can also be added to `Mount` instances, which allows you to apply middleware to a group of routes or a sub-application:
886|
887|```python
888|from starlette.applications import Starlette
889|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
890|from starlette.middleware.gzip import GZipMiddleware
891|from starlette.routing import Mount, Route
892|
893|
894|routes = [
895|    Mount(
896|        "/",
897|        routes=[
898|            Route(
899|                "/example",
900|                endpoint=...,
901|            )
902|        ],
903|        middleware=[Middleware(GZipMiddleware)]
904|    )
905|]
906|
907|app = Starlette(routes=routes)
908|```
909|
910|Note that middleware used in this way is *not* wrapped in exception handling middleware like the middleware applied to the `Starlette` application is.
911|This is often not a problem because it only applies to middleware that inspect or modify the `Response`, and even then you probably don't want to apply this logic to error responses.
912|If you do want to apply the middleware logic to error responses only on some routes you have a couple of options:
913|
914|* Add an `ExceptionMiddleware` onto the `Mount`
915|* Add a `try/except` block to your middleware and return an error response from there
916|* Split up marking and processing into two middlewares, one that gets put on `Mount` which marks the response as needing processing (for example by setting `scope["log-response"] = True`) and another applied to the `Starlette` application that does the heavy lifting.
917|
918|The `Route`/`WebSocket` class also accepts a `middleware` argument, which allows you to apply middleware to a single route:
919|
920|```python
921|from starlette.applications import Starlette
922|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
923|from starlette.middleware.gzip import GZipMiddleware
924|from starlette.routing import Route
925|
926|
927|routes = [
928|    Route(
929|        "/example",
930|        endpoint=...,
931|        middleware=[Middleware(GZipMiddleware)]
932|    )
933|]
934|
935|app = Starlette(routes=routes)
936|```
937|
938|You can also apply middleware to the `Router` class, which allows you to apply middleware to a group of routes:
939|
940|```python
941|from starlette.applications import Starlette
942|from starlette.middleware import Middleware
943|from starlette.middleware.gzip import GZipMiddleware
944|from starlette.routing import Route, Router
945|
946|
947|routes = [
948|    Route("/example", endpoint=...),
949|    Route("/another", endpoint=...),
950|]
951|
952|router = Router(routes=routes, middleware=[Middleware(GZipMiddleware)])
953|```

955|## Third party middleware
956|
957|#### [asgi-auth-github](https://github.com/simonw/asgi-auth-github)
958|
959|This middleware adds authentication to any ASGI application, requiring users to sign in
960|using their GitHub account (via [OAuth](https://developer.github.com/apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps/)).
961|Access can be restricted to specific users or to members of specific GitHub organizations or teams.
962|
963|#### [asgi-csrf](https://github.com/simonw/asgi-csrf)
964|
965|Middleware for protecting against CSRF attacks. This middleware implements the Double Submit Cookie pattern, where a cookie is set, then it is compared to a csrftoken hidden form field or an `x-csrftoken` HTTP header.
966|
967|#### [AuthlibMiddleware](https://github.com/aogier/starlette-authlib)
968|
969|A drop-in replacement for Starlette session middleware, using [authlib's jwt](https://docs.authlib.org/en/latest/jose/jwt.html)
970|module.
971|
972|#### [BugsnagMiddleware](https://github.com/ashinabraham/starlette-bugsnag)
973|
974|A middleware class for logging exceptions to [Bugsnag](https://www.bugsnag.com/).
975|
976|#### [CSRFMiddleware](https://github.com/frankie567/starlette-csrf)
977|
978|Middleware for protecting against CSRF attacks. This middleware implements the Double Submit Cookie pattern, where a cookie is set, then it is compared to an `x-csrftoken` HTTP header.
979|
980|#### [EarlyDataMiddleware](https://github.com/HarrySky/starlette-early-data)
981|
982|Middleware and decorator for detecting and denying [TLSv1.3 early data](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8470) requests.
983|
984|#### [PrometheusMiddleware](https://github.com/perdy/starlette-prometheus)
985|
986|A middleware class for capturing Prometheus metrics related to requests and responses, including in progress requests, timing...
987|
988|#### [ProxyHeadersMiddleware](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/main/uvicorn/middleware/proxy_headers.py)
989|
990|Uvicorn includes a middleware class for determining the client IP address,
991|when proxy servers are being used, based on the `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-For` headers. For more complex proxy configurations, you might want to adapt this middleware.
992|
993|#### [RateLimitMiddleware](https://github.com/abersheeran/asgi-ratelimit)
994|
995|A rate limit middleware. Regular expression matches url; flexible rules; highly customizable. Very easy to use.
996|
997|#### [RequestIdMiddleware](https://github.com/snok/asgi-correlation-id)
998|
999|A middleware class for reading/generating request IDs and attaching them to application logs.
1000|
1001|#### [RollbarMiddleware](https://docs.rollbar.com/docs/starlette)
1002|
1003|A middleware class for logging exceptions, errors, and log messages to [Rollbar](https://www.rollbar.com).
1004|
1005|#### [StarletteOpentracing](https://github.com/acidjunk/starlette-opentracing)
1006|
1007|A middleware class that emits tracing info to [OpenTracing.io](https://opentracing.io/) compatible tracers and
1008|can be used to profile and monitor distributed applications.
1009|
1010|#### [SecureCookiesMiddleware](https://github.com/thearchitector/starlette-securecookies)
1011|
1012|Customizable middleware for adding automatic cookie encryption and decryption to Starlette applications, with
1013|extra support for existing cookie-based middleware.
1014|
1015|#### [TimingMiddleware](https://github.com/steinnes/timing-asgi)
1016|
1017|A middleware class to emit timing information (cpu and wall time) for each request which
1018|passes through it.  Includes examples for how to emit these timings as statsd metrics.
1019|
1020|#### [WSGIMiddleware](https://github.com/abersheeran/a2wsgi)
1021|
1022|A middleware class in charge of converting a WSGI application into an ASGI one.

2|??? abstract "API Reference"
3|    ::: starlette.testclient.TestClient
4|        options:
5|            parameter_headings: false
6|            show_bases: false
7|            show_root_heading: true
8|            heading_level: 3
9|            filters:
10|                - "__init__"
11|
12|The test client allows you to make requests against your ASGI application,
13|using the `httpx2` library.
14|
15|!!! note
16|    The `TestClient` is built on `httpx2`. Plain `httpx` is still supported, but
17|    deprecated - install `httpx2` (included in `starlette[full]`) instead.
18|
19|```python
20|from starlette.responses import HTMLResponse
21|from starlette.testclient import TestClient
22|
23|
24|async def app(scope, receive, send):
25|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
26|    response = HTMLResponse('<html><body>Hello, world!</body></html>')
27|    await response(scope, receive, send)
28|
29|
30|def test_app():
31|    client = TestClient(app)
32|    response = client.get('/')
33|    assert response.status_code == 200
34|```
35|
36|The test client exposes the same interface as any other `httpx2` session.
37|In particular, note that the calls to make a request are just standard
38|function calls, not awaitables.
39|
40|You can use any of `httpx2` standard API, such as authentication, session
41|cookies handling, or file uploads.
42|
43|For example, to set headers on the TestClient you can do:
44|
45|```python
46|client = TestClient(app)
47|
48|# Set headers on the client for future requests
49|client.headers = {"Authorization": "..."}
50|response = client.get("/")
51|
52|# Set headers for each request separately
53|response = client.get("/", headers={"Authorization": "..."})
54|```
55|
56|And for example to send files with the TestClient:
57|
58|```python
59|client = TestClient(app)
60|
61|# Send a single file
62|with open("example.txt", "rb") as f:
63|    response = client.post("/form", files={"file": f})
64|
65|# Send multiple files
66|with open("example.txt", "rb") as f1:
67|    with open("example.png", "rb") as f2:
68|        files = {"file1": f1, "file2": ("filename", f2, "image/png")}
69|        response = client.post("/form", files=files)
70|```
71|
72|For more information you can check the `httpx2` [documentation](https://pydantic.dev/docs/httpx2/advanced/clients/).
73|
74|By default the `TestClient` will raise any exceptions that occur in the
75|application. Occasionally you might want to test the content of 500 error
76|responses, rather than allowing the client to raise the server exception. In this
77|case you should use `client = TestClient(app, raise_server_exceptions=False)`.
78|
79|!!! note
80|
81|    If you want the `TestClient` to run the `lifespan` handler,
82|    you will need to use the `TestClient` as a context manager. It will
83|    not be triggered when the `TestClient` is instantiated. You can learn more about it
84|    [here](lifespan.md#running-lifespan-in-tests).
85|
86|### HTTP trailers
87|
88|The `TestClient` supports the ASGI HTTP trailer extension. Read trailing fields from
89|`response.extensions["http.response.trailers"]` after the request completes.
90|
91|```python
92|from starlette.testclient import TestClient
93|from starlette.types import Receive, Scope, Send
94|
95|
96|async def app(scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send) -> None:
97|    await send({
98|        "type": "http.response.start", "status": 200,
99|        "headers": [(b"trailer", b"x-result")], "trailers": True,
100|    })
101|    await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"hello"})
102|    await send({"type": "http.response.trailers", "headers": [(b"x-result", b"complete")]})
103|
104|
105|def test_trailers() -> None:
106|    response = TestClient(app).get("/", headers={"TE": "trailers"})
107|    assert response.content == b"hello"
108|    assert response.extensions["http.response.trailers"] == [(b"x-result", b"complete")]
109|```
110|
111|The extension contains a list of raw byte pairs. It preserves field order and duplicates
112|across multiple trailer messages. Trailers remain separate from `response.headers`.
113|Responses that do not declare trailers have no trailer extension on the result.
114|
115|With `raise_server_exceptions=True`, invalid trailer ordering or returning without final
116|trailers raises an assertion error. With `raise_server_exceptions=False`, the result contains
117|only the trailers received before the application failed or returned.
118|
119|The test transport captures ASGI trailers regardless of `TE` negotiation. It does not emulate
120|HTTP/2 framing or concurrent request and response streaming. Use a real server and client
121|to verify those transport behaviors.
122|
123|### Debug information
124|
125|The `TestClient` supports the ASGI [`http.response.debug`](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/extensions.html#debug)
126|extension. The `info` dictionary sent by the application is available as
127|`response.extensions["http.response.debug"]`, which allows custom response classes to
128|expose additional debug information to tests.
129|
130|This is useful when asserting on the response body would mean parsing it back. Consider
131|a response class that renders rows into a CSV file. By sending the rows through the
132|debug extension, tests can assert on the original data instead of the serialized body:
133|
134|```python
135|import csv
136|import io
137|
138|from starlette.responses import Response
139|
140|
141|class CSVResponse(Response):
142|    media_type = "text/csv"
143|
144|    def __init__(self, rows):
145|        self.rows = rows
146|        buffer = io.StringIO()
147|        csv.writer(buffer).writerows(rows)
148|        super().__init__(buffer.getvalue())
149|
150|    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
151|        if "http.response.debug" in scope.get("extensions", {}):
152|            await send({"type": "http.response.debug", "info": {"rows": self.rows}})
153|        await super().__call__(scope, receive, send)
154|
155|
156|def test_export():
157|    client = TestClient(app)
158|    response = client.get("/export")
159|    rows = response.extensions["http.response.debug"]["rows"]
160|    assert rows[0] == ("id", "username", "joined")
161|    assert len(rows) == 101
162|```
163|
164|Template responses use the same extension to expose the `.template` and `.context`
165|response attributes - see [testing template responses](templates.md#testing-template-responses).
166|The `info` dictionary is always available as `response.extensions["http.response.debug"]`,
167|even when it carries `template`/`context` keys.
168|
169|### Change client address
170|
171|By default, the TestClient will set the client host to `"testclient"` and the port to `50000`.
172|
173|You can change the client address by setting the `client` attribute of the `TestClient` instance:
174|
175|```python
176|client = TestClient(app, client=('localhost', 8000))
177|```
178|
179|### Selecting the Async backend
180|
181|`TestClient` takes arguments `backend` (a string) and `backend_options` (a dictionary).
182|These options are passed to `anyio.start_blocking_portal()`.
183|See the [anyio documentation](https://anyio.readthedocs.io/en/stable/basics.html#backend-options)
184|for more information about the accepted backend options.
185|By default, `asyncio` is used with default options.
186|
187|To run `Trio`, pass `backend="trio"`. For example:
188|
189|```python
190|def test_app():
191|    with TestClient(app, backend="trio") as client:
192|       ...
193|```
194|
195|To run `asyncio` with `uvloop`, pass `backend_options={"use_uvloop": True}`.  For example:
196|
197|```python
198|def test_app():
199|    with TestClient(app, backend_options={"use_uvloop": True}) as client:
200|       ...
201|```
202|
203|### Testing WebSocket sessions
204|
205|You can also test websocket sessions with the test client.
206|
207|The `httpx2` library will be used to build the initial handshake, meaning you
208|can use the same authentication options and other headers between both http and
209|websocket testing.
210|
211|```python
212|from starlette.testclient import TestClient
213|from starlette.websockets import WebSocket
214|
215|
216|async def app(scope, receive, send):
217|    assert scope['type'] == 'websocket'
218|    websocket = WebSocket(scope, receive=receive, send=send)
219|    await websocket.accept()
220|    await websocket.send_text('Hello, world!')
221|    await websocket.close()
222|
223|
224|def test_app():
225|    client = TestClient(app)
226|    with client.websocket_connect('/') as websocket:
227|        data = websocket.receive_text()
228|        assert data == 'Hello, world!'
229|```
230|
231|The operations on session are standard function calls, not awaitables.
232|
233|It's important to use the session within a context-managed `with` block. This
234|ensures that the background thread on which the ASGI application is properly
235|terminated, and that any exceptions that occur within the application are
236|always raised by the test client.
237|
238|#### Establishing a test session
239|
240|* `.websocket_connect(url, subprotocols=None, **options)` - Takes the same set of arguments as `httpx2.get()`.
241|
242|May raise `starlette.websockets.WebSocketDisconnect` if the application does not accept the websocket connection.
243|
244|`websocket_connect()` must be used as a context manager (in a `with` block).
245|
246|!!! note
247|    The `params` argument is not supported by `websocket_connect`. If you need to pass query arguments, hard code it
248|    directly in the URL.
249|
250|    ```python
251|    with client.websocket_connect('/path?foo=bar') as websocket:
252|        ...
253|    ```
254|
255|#### Sending data
256|
257|* `.send_text(data)` - Send the given text to the application.
258|* `.send_bytes(data)` - Send the given bytes to the application.
259|* `.send_json(data, mode="text")` - Send the given data to the application. Use `mode="binary"` to send JSON over binary data frames.
260|
261|#### Receiving data
262|
263|* `.receive_text()` - Wait for incoming text sent by the application and return it.
264|* `.receive_bytes()` - Wait for incoming bytestring sent by the application and return it.
265|* `.receive_json(mode="text")` - Wait for incoming json data sent by the application and return it. Use `mode="binary"` to receive JSON over binary data frames.
266|
267|May raise `starlette.websockets.WebSocketDisconnect`.
268|
269|#### Closing the connection
270|
271|* `.close(code=1000)` - Perform a client-side close of the websocket connection.
272|
273|### Asynchronous tests
274|
275|Sometimes you will want to do async things outside of your application.
276|For example, you might want to check the state of your database after calling your app
277|using your existing async database client/infrastructure.
278|
279|For these situations, using `TestClient` is difficult because it creates its own event loop and async
280|resources (like a database connection) often cannot be shared across event loops.
281|The simplest way to work around this is to just make your entire test async and use an async client, like [httpx2.AsyncClient].
282|
283|Here is an example of such a test:
284|
285|```python
286|from httpx2 import AsyncClient, ASGITransport
287|from starlette.applications import Starlette
288|from starlette.routing import Route
289|from starlette.requests import Request
290|from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse
291|
292|
293|def hello(request: Request) -> PlainTextResponse:
294|    return PlainTextResponse("Hello World!")
295|
296|
297|app = Starlette(routes=[Route("/", hello)])
298|
299|
300|# if you're using pytest, you'll need to add an async marker like:
301|# @pytest.mark.anyio  # using https://github.com/agronholm/anyio
302|# or install and configure pytest-asyncio (https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest-asyncio)
303|async def test_app() -> None:
304|    # note: you _must_ set `base_url` for relative urls like "/" to work
305|    transport = ASGITransport(app=app)
306|    async with AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://testserver") as client:
307|        r = await client.get("/")
308|        assert r.status_code == 200
309|        assert r.text == "Hello World!"
310|```
311|
312|!!! warning "A pytest event loop fixture does not configure TestClient"
313|
314|    Defining an `event_loop` fixture does not make `TestClient` use that loop.
315|    For synchronous tests, create and close resources in [lifespan](lifespan.md#lifespan-state)
316|    and use [`TestClient` as a context manager](lifespan.md#running-lifespan-in-tests).
317|
318|[httpx2.AsyncClient]: https://pydantic.dev/docs/httpx2/advanced/transports/#asgi-transport

1|## HTTP Routing
2|
3|Starlette has a simple but capable request routing system. A routing table
4|is defined as a list of routes, and passed when instantiating the application.
5|
6|```python
7|from starlette.applications import Starlette
8|from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse
9|from starlette.routing import Route
10|
11|
12|async def homepage(request):
13|    return PlainTextResponse("Homepage")
14|
15|async def about(request):
16|    return PlainTextResponse("About")
17|
18|
19|routes = [
20|    Route("/", endpoint=homepage),
21|    Route("/about", endpoint=about),
22|]
23|
24|app = Starlette(routes=routes)
25|```
26|
27|The `endpoint` argument can be one of:
28|
29|* A regular function or async function, which accepts a single `request`
30|argument and which should return a response.
31|* A class that implements the ASGI interface, such as Starlette's [HTTPEndpoint](endpoints.md#httpendpoint).
32|
33|## Path Parameters
34|
35|Paths can use URI templating style to capture path components.
36|
37|```python
38|Route('/users/{username}', user)
39|```
40|By default this will capture characters up to the end of the path or the next `/`.
41|
42|You can use convertors to modify what is captured. The available convertors are:
43|
44|* `str` returns a string, and is the default.
45|* `int` returns a Python integer.
46|* `float` returns a Python float.
47|* `uuid` return a Python `uuid.UUID` instance.
48|* `path` returns the rest of the path, including any additional `/` characters.
49|
50|Convertors are used by prefixing them with a colon, like so:
51|
52|```python
53|Route('/users/{user_id:int}', user)
54|Route('/floating-point/{number:float}', floating_point)
55|Route('/uploaded/{rest_of_path:path}', uploaded)
56|```
57|
58|If you need a different converter that is not defined, you can create your own.
59|See below an example on how to create a `datetime` convertor, and how to register it:
60|
61|```python
62|from datetime import datetime
63|
64|from starlette.convertors import Convertor, register_url_convertor
65|
66|
67|class DateTimeConvertor(Convertor):
68|    regex = "[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}T[0-9]{2}:[0-9]{2}:[0-9]{2}(.[0-9]+)?"
69|
70|    def convert(self, value: str) -> datetime:
71|        return datetime.strptime(value, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
72|
73|    def to_string(self, value: datetime) -> str:
74|        return value.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
75|
76|register_url_convertor("datetime", DateTimeConvertor())
77|```
78|
79|After registering it, you'll be able to use it as:
80|
81|```python
82|Route('/history/{date:datetime}', history)
83|```
84|
85|Path parameters are made available in the request, as the `request.path_params`
86|dictionary.
87|
88|```python
89|async def user(request):
90|    user_id = request.path_params['user_id']
91|    ...
92|```
93|
94|## Handling HTTP methods
95|
96|Routes can also specify which HTTP methods are handled by an endpoint:
97|
98|```python
99|Route('/users/{user_id:int}', user, methods=["GET", "POST"])
100|```
101|
102|By default function endpoints will only accept `GET` requests, unless specified.
103|
104|## Submounting routes
105|
106|In large applications you might find that you want to break out parts of the
107|routing table, based on a common path prefix.
108|
109|```python
110|routes = [
111|    Route('/', homepage),
112|    Mount('/users', routes=[
113|        Route('/', users, methods=['GET', 'POST']),
114|        Route('/{username}', user),
115|    ])
116|]
117|```
118|
119|This style allows you to define different subsets of the routing table in
120|different parts of your project.
121|
122|```python
123|from myproject import users, auth
124|
125|routes = [
126|    Route('/', homepage),
127|    Mount('/users', routes=users.routes),
128|    Mount('/auth', routes=auth.routes),
129|]
130|```
131|
132|You can also use mounting to include sub-applications within your Starlette
133|application. For example...
134|
135|```python
136|# This is a standalone static files server:
137|app = StaticFiles(directory="static")
138|
139|# This is a static files server mounted within a Starlette application,
140|# underneath the "/static" path.
141|routes = [
142|    ...
143|    Mount("/static", app=StaticFiles(directory="static"), name="static")
144|]
145|
146|app = Starlette(routes=routes)
147|```
148|
149|## Reverse URL lookups
150|
151|You'll often want to be able to generate the URL for a particular route,
152|such as in cases where you need to return a redirect response.
153|
154|* Signature: `url_for(name, **path_params) -> URL`
155|
156|```python
157|routes = [
158|    Route("/", homepage, name="homepage")
159|]
160|
161|# We can use the following to return a URL...
162|url = request.url_for("homepage")
163|```
164|
165|URL lookups can include path parameters...
166|
167|```python
168|routes = [
169|    Route("/users/{username}", user, name="user_detail")
170|]
171|
172|# We can use the following to return a URL...
173|url = request.url_for("user_detail", username=...)
174|```
175|
176|If a `Mount` includes a `name`, then submounts should use a `{prefix}:{name}`
177|style for reverse URL lookups.
178|
179|```python
180|routes = [
181|    Mount("/users", name="users", routes=[
182|        Route("/", user, name="user_list"),
183|        Route("/{username}", user, name="user_detail")
184|    ])
185|]
186|
187|# We can use the following to return URLs...
188|url = request.url_for("users:user_list")
189|url = request.url_for("users:user_detail", username=...)
190|```
191|
192|Mounted applications may include a `path=...` parameter.
193|
194|```python
195|routes = [
196|    ...
197|    Mount("/static", app=StaticFiles(directory="static"), name="static")
198|]
199|
200|# We can use the following to return URLs...
201|url = request.url_for("static", path="/css/base.css")
202|```
203|
204|For cases where there is no `request` instance, you can make reverse lookups
205|against the application, although these will only return the URL path.
206|
207|```python
208|url = app.url_path_for("user_detail", username=...)
209|```
210|
211|## Host-based routing
212|
213|If you want to use different routes for the same path based on the `Host` header.
214|
215|Note that port is removed from the `Host` header when matching.
216|For example, `Host (host='example.org:3600', ...)` will be processed
217|even if the `Host` header contains or does not contain a port other than `3600`
218|(`example.org:5600`, `example.org`).
219|Therefore, you can specify the port if you need it for use in `url_for`.
220|
221|There are several ways to connect host-based routes to your application
222|
223|```python
224|site = Router(routes=[...])  # Add your `Route` entries here.
225|api = Router(routes=[...])  # Add your `Route` entries here.
226|news = Router(routes=[...])  # Add your `Route` entries here.
227|
228|routes = [
229|    Host('api.example.org', api, name="site_api")
230|]
231|
232|app = Starlette(routes=routes)
233|
234|app.host('www.example.org', site, name="main_site")
235|
236|news_host = Host('news.example.org', news)
237|app.router.routes.append(news_host)
238|```
239|
240|URL lookups can include host parameters just like path parameters
241|
242|```python
243|routes = [
244|    Host("{subdomain}.example.org", name="sub", app=Router(routes=[
245|        Mount("/users", name="users", routes=[
246|            Route("/", user, name="user_list"),
247|            Route("/{username}", user, name="user_detail")
248|        ])
249|    ]))
250|]
251|...
252|url = request.url_for("sub:users:user_detail", username=..., subdomain=...)
253|url = request.url_for("sub:users:user_list", subdomain=...)
254|```
255|
256|## Route priority
257|
258|Incoming paths are matched against each `Route` in order.
259|
260|In cases where more that one route could match an incoming path, you should
261|take care to ensure that more specific routes are listed before general cases.
262|
263|For example:
264|
265|```python
266|# Don't do this: `/users/me` will never match incoming requests.
267|routes = [
268|    Route('/users/{username}', user),
269|    Route('/users/me', current_user),
270|]
271|
272|# Do this: `/users/me` is tested first.
273|routes = [
274|    Route('/users/me', current_user),
275|    Route('/users/{username}', user),
276|]
277|```
278|
279|## Working with Router instances
280|
281|If you're working at a low-level you might want to use a plain `Router`
282|instance, rather that creating a `Starlette` application. This gives you
283|a lightweight ASGI application that just provides the application routing,
284|without wrapping it up in any middleware.
285|
286|```python
287|app = Router(routes=[
288|    Route('/', homepage),
289|    Mount('/users', routes=[
290|        Route('/', users, methods=['GET', 'POST']),
291|        Route('/{username}', user),
292|    ])
293|])
294|```
295|
296|## Request body size limits
297|
298|Use a non-negative `max_body_size` to limit the total number of request body
299|bytes accepted by an application. The limit includes multipart file data and
300|multipart encoding overhead. It defaults to `None`, which preserves the existing
301|unlimited behavior.
302|
303|```python
304|app = Starlette(
305|    routes=[
306|        Route("/", homepage),
307|        Route("/upload", upload, methods=["POST"], max_body_size=100 * 1024 * 1024),
308|    ],
309|    max_body_size=10 * 1024 * 1024,
310|)
311|```
312|
313|`Router` and `Mount` also accept `max_body_size`. A limit on an inner route,
314|mount, or router overrides the outer limit after routing. This allows an upload
315|route to accept a larger body than the rest of the application.
316|
317|Application middleware runs before routing. If such middleware reads the body,
318|the application-level limit applies to those bytes before a route can raise the
319|limit. Keep the application limit large enough for the largest legitimate route
320|when using body-consuming application middleware.
321|
322|Starlette counts the actual body bytes received from the ASGI server.
323|`Content-Length` is used only to reject an oversized request early and is not
324|trusted to enforce the limit. A reverse proxy request-body limit and a quota on
325|temporary storage provide additional deployment-level safeguards.
326|
327|## WebSocket Routing
328|
329|When working with WebSocket endpoints, you should use `WebSocketRoute`
330|instead of the usual `Route`.
331|
332|Path parameters, and reverse URL lookups for `WebSocketRoute` work the same
333|as HTTP `Route`, which can be found in the HTTP [Route](#http-routing) section above.
334|
335|```python
336|from starlette.applications import Starlette
337|from starlette.routing import WebSocketRoute
338|
339|
340|async def websocket_index(websocket):
341|    await websocket.accept()
342|    await websocket.send_text("Hello, websocket!")
343|    await websocket.close()
344|
345|
346|async def websocket_user(websocket):
347|    name = websocket.path_params["name"]
348|    await websocket.accept()
349|    await websocket.send_text(f"Hello, {name}")
350|    await websocket.close()
351|
352|
353|routes = [
354|    WebSocketRoute("/", endpoint=websocket_index),
355|    WebSocketRoute("/{name}", endpoint=websocket_user),
356|]
357|
358|app = Starlette(routes=routes)
359|```
360|
361|The `endpoint` argument can be one of:
362|
363|* An async function, which accepts a single `websocket` argument.
364|* A class that implements the ASGI interface, such as Starlette's [WebSocketEndpoint](endpoints.md#websocketendpoint).

--- FILE: docs/responses.md ---
1|
2|Starlette includes a few response classes that handle sending back the
3|appropriate ASGI messages on the `send` channel.
4|
5|### Response
6|
7|Signature: `Response(content, status_code=200, headers=None, media_type=None)`
8|
9|* `content` - A string or bytestring.
10|* `status_code` - An integer HTTP status code.
11|* `headers` - A dictionary of strings.
12|* `media_type` - A string giving the media type. eg. "text/html"
13|
14|Starlette will automatically include a Content-Length header. It will also
15|include a Content-Type header, based on the media_type and appending a charset
16|for text types, unless a charset has already been specified in the `media_type`.
17|
18|Once you've instantiated a response, you can send it by calling it as an
19|ASGI application instance.
20|
21|```python
22|from starlette.responses import Response
23|
24|
25|async def app(scope, receive, send):
26|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
27|    response = Response('Hello, world!', media_type='text/plain')
28|    await response(scope, receive, send)
29|```
30|#### Set Cookie
31|
32|Starlette provides a `set_cookie` method to allow you to set cookies on the response object.
33|
34|Signature: `Response.set_cookie(key, value, max_age=None, expires=None, path="/", domain=None, secure=False, httponly=False, samesite="lax", partitioned=False)`
35|
36|* `key` - A string that will be the cookie's key.
37|* `value` - A string that will be the cookie's value.
38|* `max_age` - An integer that defines the lifetime of the cookie in seconds. A negative integer or a value of `0` will discard the cookie immediately. `Optional`
39|* `expires` - Either an integer that defines the number of seconds until the cookie expires, or a datetime. `Optional`
40|* `path` - A string that specifies the subset of routes to which the cookie will apply. `Optional`
41|* `domain` - A string that specifies the domain for which the cookie is valid. `Optional`
42|* `secure` - A bool indicating that the cookie will only be sent to the server if request is made using SSL and the HTTPS protocol. `Optional`
43|* `httponly` - A bool indicating that the cookie cannot be accessed via JavaScript through `Document.cookie` property, the `XMLHttpRequest` or `Request` APIs. `Optional`
44|* `samesite` - A string that specifies the samesite strategy for the cookie. Valid values are `'lax'`, `'strict'` and `'none'`. Defaults to `'lax'`. `Optional`
45|* `partitioned` - A bool that indicates to user agents that these cross-site cookies should only be available in the same top-level context that the cookie was first set in. Only available for Python 3.14+, otherwise an error will be raised. `Optional`
46|
47|#### Delete Cookie
48|
49|Conversely, Starlette also provides a `delete_cookie` method to manually expire a set cookie.
50|
51|Signature: `Response.delete_cookie(key, path='/', domain=None, secure=False, httponly=False, samesite="lax", partitioned=False)`
52|
53|To delete a partitioned cookie on Python 3.14+:
54|
55|```python
56|from starlette.responses import Response
57|
58|response = Response()
59|response.delete_cookie("session", secure=True, samesite="none", partitioned=True)
60|```
61|
62|Pass `partitioned=True` to expire the cookie in the current partition. It defaults to `False`.
63|Use the same `path` and `domain` as the original cookie, within the same top-level site context.
64|For cross-site requests, use `samesite="none"`.
65|
66|!!! warning "Partitioned cookies require Secure"
67|    Pass `secure=True` when deleting a partitioned cookie over HTTPS.
68|    Browsers reject the expiration header if it includes `Partitioned` without `Secure`.
69|
70|
71|### HTMLResponse
72|
73|Takes some text or bytes and returns an HTML response.
74|
75|```python
76|from starlette.responses import HTMLResponse
77|
78|
79|async def app(scope, receive, send):
80|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
81|    response = HTMLResponse('<html><body><h1>Hello, world!</h1></body></html>')
82|    await response(scope, receive, send)
83|```
84|
85|### PlainTextResponse
86|
87|Takes some text or bytes and returns a plain text response.
88|
89|```python
90|from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse
91|
92|
93|async def app(scope, receive, send):
94|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
95|    response = PlainTextResponse('Hello, world!')
96|    await response(scope, receive, send)
97|```
98|
99|### JSONResponse
100|
101|Takes some data and returns an `application/json` encoded response.
102|
103|```python
104|from starlette.responses import JSONResponse
105|
106|
107|async def app(scope, receive, send):
108|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
109|    response = JSONResponse({'hello': 'world'})
110|    await response(scope, receive, send)
111|```
112|
113|#### Custom JSON serialization
114|
115|If you need fine-grained control over JSON serialization, you can subclass
116|`JSONResponse` and override the `render` method.
117|
118|For example, if you wanted to use a third-party JSON library such as
119|[orjson](https://pypi.org/project/orjson/):
120|
121|```python
122|from typing import Any
123|
124|import orjson
125|from starlette.responses import JSONResponse
126|
127|
128|class OrjsonResponse(JSONResponse):
129|    def render(self, content: Any) -> bytes:
130|        return orjson.dumps(content)
131|```
132|
133|In general you *probably* want to stick with `JSONResponse` by default unless
134|you are micro-optimising a particular endpoint or need to serialize non-standard
135|object types.
136|
137|### RedirectResponse
138|
139|Returns an HTTP redirect. Uses a 307 status code by default.
140|
141|```python
142|from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse, RedirectResponse
143|
144|
145|async def app(scope, receive, send):
146|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
147|    if scope['path'] != '/':
148|        response = RedirectResponse(url='/')
149|    else:
150|        response = PlainTextResponse('Hello, world!')
151|    await response(scope, receive, send)
152|```
153|
154|### StreamingResponse
155|
156|Takes an async generator or a normal generator/iterator and streams the response body.
157|
158|```python
159|from starlette.responses import StreamingResponse
160|import asyncio
161|
162|
163|async def slow_numbers(minimum, maximum):
164|    yield '<html><body><ul>'
165|    for number in range(minimum, maximum + 1):
166|        yield '<li>%d</li>' % number
167|        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
168|    yield '</ul></body></html>'
169|
170|
171|async def app(scope, receive, send):
172|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
173|    generator = slow_numbers(1, 10)
174|    response = StreamingResponse(generator, media_type='text/html')
175|    await response(scope, receive, send)
176|```
177|
178|Have in mind that <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-file-like-object" target="_blank">file-like</a> objects (like those created by `open()`) are normal iterators. So, you can return them directly in a `StreamingResponse`.
179|
180|### FileResponse
181|
182|Asynchronously streams a file as the response.
183|
184|Takes a different set of arguments to instantiate than the other response types:
185|
186|* `path` - The filepath to the file to stream.
187|* `headers` - Any custom headers to include, as a dictionary.
188|* `media_type` - A string giving the media type. If unset, the filename or path will be used to infer a media type.
189|* `filename` - If set, this will be included in the response `Content-Disposition`.
190|* `content_disposition_type` - will be included in the response `Content-Disposition`. Can be set to "attachment" (default) or "inline".
191|
192|File responses will include appropriate `Content-Length`, `Last-Modified` and `ETag` headers.
193|
194|```python
195|from starlette.responses import FileResponse
196|
197|
198|async def app(scope, receive, send):
199|    assert scope['type'] == 'http'
200|    response = FileResponse('statics/favicon.ico')
201|    await response(scope, receive, send)
202|```
203|
204|File responses also supports [HTTP range requests](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Range_requests).
205|
206|The `Accept-Ranges: bytes` header will be included in the response if the file exists. For now, only the `bytes`
207|range unit is supported.
208|
209|If the request includes a `Range` header, and the file exists, the response will be a `206 Partial Content` response
210|with the requested range of bytes. If the range is invalid, the response will be a `416 Range Not Satisfiable` response.
211|
212|## Third party responses
213|
214|#### [EventSourceResponse](https://github.com/sysid/sse-starlette)
215|
216|A response class that implements [Server-Sent Events](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html). It enables event streaming from the server to the client without the complexity of websockets.
